sections.title: 13.1 Network Security Threats and the Three Primary Attacks

content.text: Book pages 365 to 366. Start with vocabulary the objective names: threat (something that can cause harm), vulnerability (a weakness), exploit (a way of using the weakness), mitigation (what you do about it). ADDED
Four types of threat actor
| Threat | Who | Note |
| Unstructured | Curious people, script kiddies using tools found online | Not very skilled, often for thrills. |
| Structured | Skilled, dedicated attackers who understand network design | Can write their own scripts; repeat offenders. |
| External | From outside, usually via the Internet | Enter through holes in the perimeter. |
| Internal | Employees and contractors | Hardest to stop, because they are already authorised and know the network. |
Three primary attack categories
| Category | Goal | Example |
| Reconnaissance | Discover and map the network, resources and weaknesses. Often a first step. | Scanning, sniffing. |
| Access | Get data, gain access or raise privileges. | Finding an unprotected network share; password guessing. |
| Denial of service (DoS) | Stop legitimate users from using the service by crashing or overloading it. | SYN flood, ping flood. |
EXAM CRITICAL
Recon = learn. Access = get in. DoS = knock out. If an exam stem says "mapping the network", the answer is reconnaissance. BOOK
Quick check 13.1
Q1. Which threat type is the hardest to stop, according to the book?
A. Unstructured
B. Structured
C. External
D. Internal
Answer: D - internal users are already authorised.
Q2. A port scan to list open services is which attack category?
Answer: Reconnaissance - it discovers, it does not yet attack.
Q3. What is a vulnerability, in one line?
Answer: A weakness that could be used to cause harm - an exploit is the way of using it.
Book pages 366 to 374. The book lists 13 common attacks. Learn each one as: what it is, and how to reduce it.
| Attack | What it is BOOK | Mitigation BOOK |

| Eavesdropping (snooping, sniffing) | Reading packets crossing the network. Clear-text protocols such as POP3 expose passwords (the book shows USER and PASS in a capture). | Encrypt sensitive traffic; forbid protocols that send credentials in clear text. |

| Denial of service | Overwhelm a server or bandwidth. Includes TCP session flooding, ICMP floods, SYN flood, chargen (UDP flood), fragmentation attacks, e-mail bombs, land.c (source = destination). | Cisco TCP intercept for SYN floods; firewall features; monitoring. You cannot stop DoS completely. |
| Unauthorized access | Gaining root or administrator rights; adding back-door accounts. | AAA with TACACS+, CHAP, and Lock and Key (legacy). |
| WareZ | Unauthorised distribution of software (piracy). | Activation keys and licensing. |
| Masquerade (IP spoofing) | Outsider uses an address inside your range to look trusted. | ACL on the Internet-facing interface that denies your own internal addresses coming in. |
| Session hijacking or replaying | Taking over or replaying a TCP session. | Strongly authenticated, encrypted management protocols. |
| Rerouting | Changing routing tables to send traffic to the attacker. | Access control; ASA or Firepower. |
| Repudiation | Denying a transaction by erasing or altering logs. Non-repudiation is the opposite: you can prove it happened. | Logging, authentication, digital signatures. |

| Smurf (and fraggle) | Echo requests to a broadcast address with the victim's address as source; every host replies to the victim. Fraggle uses UDP echo. | Filter spoofed source addresses at the network edge. |
| Password attacks | Brute force: a program tries many passwords. | Strong passwords, lockouts, MFA. |
| Man-in-the-middle | Attacker sits between two parties to steal, hijack, alter or analyse traffic. | Encryption and authentication. |
| Application-layer attacks | Exploit well-known weaknesses in applications (the book names Sendmail, PostScript, FTP). | Patching; least privilege. |
| Trojans, viruses, worms | Trojan disguises itself as a useful program. A virus needs human action to spread; a worm spreads by itself. | Updated anti-virus and anti-malware. |
| HTML attacks | Malicious Java applets or ActiveX loaded through the browser. | Browser security settings. |
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE
Dated material in the attack text. UPDATED

1. Java blocking, ActiveX, CBAC and Lock and Key are legacy. Java applets and ActiveX have been removed from modern browsers. Context-Based Access Control has largely been replaced by zone-based firewalls and Cisco's newer firewall products. Lock and Key (dynamic ACLs) is rarely used. The book still lists them and its review answer 13 expects Lock and Key. Learn them for the book's questions, not for real designs. CHECK

2. The book calls smurf "the latest trend". It is an old attack. Modern IOS leaves directed broadcasts off by default (no ip directed-broadcast), which stops the router forwarding the broadcast. ADDED CHECK
3. The book says audit logs are useful so you can "send them to the FBI". Logs help any investigation; there is no exam value in the law-enforcement point.

4. The ICMP "Ping of Death" is described loosely. Treat it as: oversized or malformed ICMP packets that crash a vulnerable system, and ping floods that overload it. Current systems are patched against the malformed-packet version. CHECK

5. The Exam Essentials sentence "spoofing, man-in-the-middle and session replaying" lists the weaknesses the book wants you to remember. Review question 11 asks for session replaying, SNMP and SMTP as TCP/IP weaknesses. Both are the book's view; SNMPv1/v2c and plain SMTP are weak because they are unencrypted or weakly authenticated. BOOK
MEMORY TIP
Memory hook for DoS: SYN flood, Chargen, Land, E-mail bomb, Fragmentation, Ping (floods). Not an official list; a way to remember the book's items. ADDED
Quick check 13.2
Q1. Which Cisco IOS feature protects TCP servers from SYN floods?
A. Lock and Key
B. TCP intercept
C. CBAC
D. CHAP
Answer: B - the book's review answer 12.
Q2. Which control stops outside attackers from spoofing your internal addresses?
Answer: An ACL on the Internet-facing interface denying your internal range as source - the book's masquerade fix.
Q3. What is the difference between a virus and a worm?
Answer: A virus needs human action to spread; a worm spreads by itself - both replicate.
Q4. Which attack sends echo requests to a broadcast address using the victim's address as source?
Answer: Smurf - fraggle is the UDP version.
Q5. Which term means you can prove a communication took place?
Answer: Non-repudiation - repudiation is denying it.
Book pages 374 to 377. A security program backed by a security policy has three key elements: user awareness, training and physical access control. BOOK
User awareness: social engineering
| Term | Meaning |
| Phishing | Fake messages or sites that trick users into giving credentials or financial data. Spear phishing targets one person using background research. |
| Pharming | Poisoning DNS (for example a computer's DNS cache) so a legitimate name leads to a fake site. |
| Shoulder surfing | Watching someone type or read sensitive data. |
| Dumpster diving | Searching trash for information. |
| Identity theft | Using stolen personal data to impersonate someone. |
Malware classes
| Class | Meaning |
| Virus | Attaches itself to another application to replicate. |
| Worm | Replicates without another program or human action. |
| Trojan horse | Disguised as a needed application while doing harm. |
| Spyware | Collects private data such as browsing history or keystrokes. |
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

The book tells users to check the padlock or HTTPS in the address bar to confirm a site is genuine. That is not reliable: phishing sites can also use HTTPS. The padlock means the connection is encrypted, not that the site is trustworthy. Check the full domain name. The book also says SSL; modern HTTPS uses TLS. UPDATED
Training

User security-awareness training is the best countermeasure against social engineering. It should be required and repeated regularly, because techniques change. Warn users not to follow links in e-mail.
Physical access control
| Control | Key point |
| Mantrap | Two doors with a small room between. Authenticate at door 1, verify again before door 2. Very high security. |
| Badge reader (RFID) | Needs the physical badge. Drawback: a lost or stolen badge works for anyone. |
| Smart card | Embedded identity and rights; hard to counterfeit, easy to steal. Often needs a PIN; avoid identifying marks on the card. |
| Security guard | Human judgement; can spot what automated systems miss. |
| Door lock | The most universal barrier. Use multiple barriers: outer = fence and perimeter; middle = guards, locks and mantraps; inner = key fobs and smart cards to the computer room. |
EXAM CRITICAL

Three elements: user awareness, training, physical access control. The book's review question 10 ("which is not") expects smart card, because a smart card is one example of physical control, not an element of the program. BOOK
Quick check 13.3
Q1. Name the three security program elements.
Answer: User awareness, training and physical access control - the book's list.
Q2. What is the difference between phishing and pharming?
Answer: Phishing tricks the user; pharming redirects them by corrupting DNS - pharming does not need the user to click a bad link.
Q3. Which physical control uses two interlocking doors?
A. Smart card
B. Mantrap
C. Badge reader
D. Door lock
Answer: B - a small room between two doors.

Book pages 378 to 380. The Access Layer is where user devices plug in, so it is where users and attackers meet the network. The book names four ways to protect it: port security, DHCP snooping, Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) and identity-based networking. BOOK
| Feature | Purpose BOOK |
| Port security | Limits a port to a specific set of MAC addresses. |
| DHCP snooping | Acts like a firewall between trusted hosts and untrusted DHCP servers. Interfaces are trusted or untrusted. Builds the DHCP snooping binding database. |
| Dynamic ARP Inspection | Checks ARP packets against the IP-to-MAC bindings learned by DHCP snooping, to stop ARP poisoning. |
| Identity-based networking (802.1X) | Authenticates the user when they connect and applies VLAN and policy by identity. |
DHCP snooping
- Trusted interfaces (to the real DHCP server, or an uplink towards it) allow all DHCP messages. BOOK
- Untrusted interfaces (user ports) only permit requests. Offers and acknowledgements arriving on an untrusted port are dropped. BOOK
- The binding database holds: MAC address, IP address, lease time, binding type, VLAN and interface. BOOK
- DAI uses this database. You need DHCP snooping before DAI works. BOOK
Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI)
- On an untrusted port, each ARP packet is checked: does this sender IP match this sender MAC in the binding table? If not, it is dropped. BOOK
- Protects against ARP poisoning, which is how a man-in-the-middle attack is often set up on a LAN. BOOK
- Hosts with static IP addresses are not in the DHCP table; they need an ARP ACL or a static binding. ADDED CHECK
Identity-based networking and 802.1X

IEEE 802.1X lets a switch authenticate a user at the port, then place the user in the right VLAN and policy. Failed users may go to a guest VLAN or be refused. The book says Cisco ISE and DNA Center are identity-based networking products. BOOK
| 802.1X role | What it is BOOK |
| Client (supplicant) | 802.1X-capable software on the device being connected. |
| Authenticator | Usually a switch (or wireless AP or VPN server). Controls physical access and relays between client and server. |
| Authentication server | Normally RADIUS. Authenticates each client before any services are available. |
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE
The book writes "ISE (Identity Security Engine)". The product is Identity Services Engine. UPDATED
The book does not name the protocol between client and switch (EAPOL, EAP over LAN). The switch then carries the credentials to RADIUS. ADDED CHECK
Configuration commands the book omits
VERIFY

Objective 5.7 says "configure". The book shows none of these. Commands below are from Cisco-style guides and tutorials (secondary sources) and were not run by me. Interface names and VLANs are examples. ADDED CHECK
Port security
Port security ADDED CHECK
SW1(config)# interface fastEthernet 0/1
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if)# switchport port-security
SW1(config-if)# switchport port-security maximum 2
SW1(config-if)# switchport port-security mac-address sticky
SW1(config-if)# switchport port-security violation shutdown
SW1# show port-security
SW1# show port-security interface fastEthernet 0/1
- switchport mode access: the port must be a static access port first.
- switchport port-security: turns it on. Defaults are generally one allowed MAC and violation mode shutdown. CHECK
- maximum 2: allow up to two MAC addresses on this port.
- mac-address sticky: learn MACs dynamically and save them in the running-config.
- violation shutdown: err-disable the port on a violation. Recover with shutdown then no shutdown.
| Violation mode | Drops offending frames | Logs / counts | Port shut down |
| protect | Yes | No log | No |
| restrict | Yes | Yes (log and counter) | No |
| shutdown (default) | Yes | Yes | Yes (err-disabled) |
DHCP snooping
DHCP snooping ADDED CHECK
SW1(config)# ip dhcp snooping
SW1(config)# ip dhcp snooping vlan 10,20
SW1(config)# interface gigabitEthernet 0/1
SW1(config-if)# ip dhcp snooping trust
SW1(config)# interface range fastEthernet 0/2 - 24
SW1(config-if-range)# ip dhcp snooping limit rate 15
SW1# show ip dhcp snooping
SW1# show ip dhcp snooping binding
- ip dhcp snooping: turns it on globally. It does nothing until you also list VLANs.
- ip dhcp snooping vlan 10,20: the VLANs it protects.
- ip dhcp snooping trust: uplink and DHCP server ports only. Forget this and DHCP breaks for everybody.
- limit rate 15: packets per second allowed on an untrusted port.
- show ip dhcp snooping binding: the binding table.
Dynamic ARP Inspection
DAI ADDED CHECK
SW1(config)# ip arp inspection vlan 10,20
SW1(config)# interface gigabitEthernet 0/1
SW1(config-if)# ip arp inspection trust
SW1(config)# ip arp inspection validate src-mac dst-mac ip
SW1# show ip arp inspection
SW1# show ip arp inspection interfaces
- ip arp inspection vlan 10,20: enable DAI in those VLANs (needs DHCP snooping bindings).
- ip arp inspection trust: trust the uplink. ARP from trusted ports is not checked.
- validate src-mac dst-mac ip: extra sanity checks on each ARP packet.
COMMON MISTAKE

Trusting the wrong ports. User-facing ports must stay untrusted for both DHCP snooping and DAI. Only uplinks and the DHCP server's port are trusted. Also, a device that lets users set up a DHCP server or static IPs will be blocked unless you account for it.
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

Option 82. When a switch with snooping enabled receives DHCP traffic from a router acting as DHCP server, the DHCP relay information option can cause drops. Tutorials often add no ip dhcp snooping information option on a flat segment. Test in your lab before relying on it. ADDED CHECK
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

Answer key problem (review question 3). The key says the two untrue statements are C and D. Its own explanation, though, says DHCP snooping does rate-limit DHCP. A careful reading: rate limiting is applied per untrusted port, so "from trusted and untrusted sources" (C) is untrue; the binding database lists leases to hosts on untrusted ports, so B ("trusted hosts") is also doubtful. The book's description of snooping as a firewall "between trusted hosts and untrusted DHCP servers" makes D ("between hosts") loosely worded. Do not rely on this question for study. UPDATED CHECK
Quick check 13.4
Q1. Which feature must be running for DAI to build its IP-to-MAC checks?
A. Port security
B. DHCP snooping
D. Storm control
Answer: B - the binding database comes from DHCP snooping.
Q2. Which switch ports should be DHCP-snooping trusted?
Answer: The port to the real DHCP server and uplinks toward it - never user ports.
Q3. Which port-security violation mode shuts the port down?
Answer: shutdown - it is the default mode.
Q4. Which three 802.1X roles does the book name?
Answer: Client (supplicant), authenticator, authentication server - RADIUS is the usual server.
Q5. A rogue DHCP server is plugged into an access port. What happens with snooping on?
Answer: Its DHCP offers are dropped on the untrusted port - only trusted ports may send offers.

sections.title: 13.5 Securing Network Access with Cisco AAA

content.text: Book page 380. AAA gives systematic access control, locally or remotely. BOOK
| Letter | Question it answers | Book detail BOOK |
| Authentication | Who are you? | Prove identity by name and password, challenge and response, or token cards. |
| Authorization | What may you do? | Happens only after authentication. Gives the resources and operations a user is allowed. |
| Accounting (and auditing) | What did you do? | Records activity, resources used and time spent. |
EXAM CRITICAL
Order: authenticate first, then authorize, then account. Authorization cannot happen before authentication. BOOK
MEMORY TIP
Quick test: login prompt = authentication. "This user can run show but not configure" = authorization. "Log every command typed" = accounting. ADDED
Quick check 13.5
Q1. A log shows which commands each admin typed. Which AAA function is that?
Answer: Accounting - it records what the user did.
Q2. Which comes first: authorization or authentication?
Answer: Authentication - you must prove identity first.
Book pages 381 to 386. The book ranks username and password methods from weakest to strongest. BOOK
| Method | Notes BOOK |
| No username or password | No security at all. |
| Static username and password | Fixed until the admin changes it. Easy to snoop. |
| Aging username and password | Expires after a set time (often 30 to 90 days). Still open to replay, eavesdropping and cracking. |
| One-time passwords (OTP) | Each password good for one login. Often generated from a secret pass-phrase (S/KEY). |
| Token cards and soft tokens | A device or phone app generates an OTP that the token server checks. The book calls this the most secure of the list. |
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

Token cards are not "the most secure" today. A one-time code can still be phished. Current guidance favours phishing-resistant methods such as FIDO2 security keys and certificates. For the exam, the book's order (none, static, aging, OTP, token) is what a question may use. UPDATED CHECK
Windows and security-server authentication
- Windows users log in locally or remotely (PPP and TCP/IP to a security server). A AAA server can check credentials against the Microsoft Active Directory user database. BOOK
- Cisco AAA can use a local database (fine for one or two devices) or a remote security server. BOOK
- With 300 routers, changing a password locally means touching all 300. A central server solves that. BOOK
- Cisco routers support three security-server protocols: RADIUS, TACACS+ and Kerberos. BOOK
- AAA flow (book Figure 13.6): 1 client requests login, 2 device queries the AAA server, 3 server responds, 4 device accepts or rejects. BOOK
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

The book (page 383) says the router submits credentials to "the ISE security server". ISE is one product that can act as a RADIUS or TACACS+ server; so can others. The AAA protocols are the point. UPDATED
RADIUS
- Developed by the IETF. Open standard, supported by most vendors. BOOK
- Uses UDP only. BOOK Standard ports are UDP 1812 (authentication) and 1813 (accounting). Older systems used 1645 and 1646. ADDED CHECK
- Combines authentication and authorization in one process. BOOK
- Client is the router, switch or AP; server is a Windows or Unix machine running RADIUS. BOOK
- Encrypts only the password in the access-request packet. The rest of the packet is clear. BOOK
| RADIUS reply | Meaning BOOK |
| Accept | User authenticated. |
| Reject | Username or password not valid. |
| Challenge | Server wants more information. |
| Change Password | User must pick a new password. |
Book: configuring RADIUS
Book configuration BOOK
Router(config)# aaa new-model
Router(config)# username Todd password Lammle
Router(config)# radius server SecureLogin
Router(config-radius-server)# address ipv4 10.10.10.254
Router(config-radius-server)# key MyRadiusPassword
Router(config)# aaa group server radius MyRadiusGroup
Router(config-sg-radius)# server name SecureLogin
Router(config)# aaa authentication login default group MyRadiusGroup local

- aaa new-model: turns on the AAA commands. The book says it immediately applies local authentication to all lines and interfaces except line con 0. Create a local user before turning it on to avoid locking yourself out. BOOK CHECK
- username Todd password Lammle: local fallback user. Use secret instead (see the corrections). UPDATED
- radius server SecureLogin and address ipv4 ... and key ...: defines the server and the shared key.
- aaa group server radius MyRadiusGroup + server name SecureLogin: puts the server in a named group.
- aaa authentication login default group MyRadiusGroup local: for logins, ask the RADIUS group first; if it does not answer, use the local database.
EXAM CRITICAL
The word local at the end of the method list is the fallback. Review question 6's correct answer has default, then the group, then local. BOOK
COMMON MISTAKE
Fallback only happens when the server is unreachable. If the RADIUS server answers with Reject, the login fails; the router does not try local. ADDED CHECK
TACACS+
- Terminal Access Controller Access Control System Plus. Uses TCP. BOOK Standard port is TCP 49. ADDED CHECK
- Separates authentication, authorization and accounting. You can control each one on its own. BOOK
- The Exam Essentials call it "Cisco proprietary". BOOK
|  | RADIUS | TACACS+ |
| Origin | IETF, open standard | Cisco-originated (book: Cisco proprietary) |
| Transport | UDP (1812 and 1813) | TCP (49) |
| AAA services | Authentication and authorization combined | Separate A, A and A |
| Encryption | Password only in access-request | The book does not say; commonly the whole packet body is encrypted CHECK |
| Typical use | Network access (802.1X, VPN, Wi-Fi) | Device administration (commands, privilege levels) ADDED |
Book: configuring TACACS+ (as printed)
The book's printed commands; do not copy the first lines BOOK UPDATED
Router(config)# tacacs-server SecureLoginTACACS+
Router(config-radius-server)# address ipv4 10.10.10.254
Router(config-radius-server)# key MyTACACS+Password
Router(config)# aaa group server tacacs+ MyTACACS+Group
Router(config-sg-radius)# server name SecureLoginTACACS+
Router(config)# aaa authentication login default group MyTACACS+Group local
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

Printed syntax error. The book writes tacacs-server SecureLoginTACACS+ and shows the config-radius-server prompt (a copy-and-paste from the RADIUS example). On current IOS the command is tacacs server <name> and the prompt is config-server-tacacs. The older tacacs-server host form is legacy. Also avoid the + sign in your own names. Corrected version below. UPDATED CHECK
Corrected TACACS+ configuration UPDATED CHECK
Router(config)# tacacs server SecureLoginTACACS
Router(config-server-tacacs)# address ipv4 10.10.10.254
Router(config-server-tacacs)# key MyTACACSKey
Router(config-server-tacacs)# exit
Router(config)# aaa group server tacacs+ MyTACACSGroup
Router(config-sg-tacacs+)# server name SecureLoginTACACS
Router(config-sg-tacacs+)# exit
Router(config)# aaa authentication login default group MyTACACSGroup local
Authorization and accounting (the book shows only authentication) ADDED CHECK
Router(config)# aaa authorization exec default group MyTACACSGroup local
Router(config)# aaa accounting exec default start-stop group MyTACACSGroup
- aaa authorization exec default group MyTACACSGroup local: ask the server what the user may do after login; fall back to local.
- aaa accounting exec default start-stop group MyTACACSGroup: record the start and stop of each exec session.
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

The book says TACACS+ was "developed by Cisco and later released as an open standard", and elsewhere that it is Cisco proprietary. It was created by Cisco and later documented publicly (RFC 8907, 2020). For the exam: TACACS+ = Cisco proprietary, TCP, separates AAA. The book's phrase "multiprotocol support" (review answer 4) refers to old protocols such as AppleTalk and is no longer relevant. UPDATED CHECK
Kerberos (in the authentication list)
Covered in Section 13.9. The book lists it as the third security-server protocol supported by Cisco routers. BOOK
Quick check 13.6
Q1. Which command enables the AAA commands on a router or switch?
A. aaa enable
B. enable aaa
C. new-model aaa
D. aaa new-model
Answer: D - the book's review answer 1.
Q2. Which protocol uses TCP and separates authentication, authorization and accounting?
Answer: TACACS+ - RADIUS uses UDP and combines authentication and authorization.
Q3. What does local at the end of aaa authentication login default group MyRadiusGroup local do?
Answer: Gives a fallback to the local user database if the RADIUS server does not respond - no answer from the server.
Q4. Which parts of a RADIUS access-request are encrypted?
Answer: Only the password - the rest is clear.
Q5. Why create a local user before aaa new-model?
Answer: So you cannot be locked out - without it you may need password recovery.
Book pages 386 to 389. Good authentication fails if accounts are badly managed. BOOK
| Topic | What the book says |

| Disabling accounts | When someone leaves you can leave, delete or disable the account. Disable is best. Leaving it lets anyone with the password in; deleting loses the numeric ID (UID or SID), so a new account with the same name gets none of the old rights. Use account expiry dates for temporary staff. |
| Anonymous accounts | A shared guest login with very limited access (public Wi-Fi, FTP). Hard to track. Keep Windows Guest disabled unless needed. |
| Limiting connections | Normally one simultaneous login per user; more than one suggests someone else is using the account. |
| Renaming the maintenance account | Rename Administrator (Windows) and root (Unix). The book lists names to avoid: Admin, Administrator, Root, Super, Superuser, Manager and similar. |
EXAM CRITICAL
Account clean-up rule: disable first, decide later. BOOK
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

On network gear the equivalent habits are: no shared accounts, named accounts per admin, AAA accounting to see who did what, and no default usernames or passwords. Renaming the Unix root account is rarely practical; disabling direct root login is more common. ADDED CHECK
Quick check 13.7
Q1. Which is the best way to handle an account when an employee leaves?
A. Leave it
B. Delete it
C. Disable it
D. Rename it to Guest
Answer: C - keeps the ID and settings without allowing logins.
Q2. Why limit simultaneous connections?
Answer: Two places at once suggests someone else is using the account - per the book.

Book pages 389 to 398. This is objective 5.4: password management, complexity and alternatives. The book's advice and current guidance disagree in places. Learn both: what an exam may ask, and what is considered good practice today.
Password management
How many possible passwords? (arithmetic checked by script)
| Length | 62 characters (a-z, A-Z, 0-9) | 26 characters (a-z) |
All book figures match the script. Each extra character multiplies the possibilities, so length matters most. BOOK ADDED
| Policy item | Book says BOOK | Current guidance UPDATED |

| Length | At least 10 characters if security matters; elsewhere "at least 8, no more than 15". | Longer is better. Do not cap length low; allow at least 64 characters. NIST suggests 15 or more for single-factor passwords and 8 as a minimum with MFA. CHECK |

| Complexity | Mix upper, lower, numbers, symbols. (It also notes NIST prefers length over complexity.) | NIST says do not impose composition rules; check against lists of common and breached passwords instead. CHECK |
| Expiration | Change every 30 days (or 30 to 45); keep a password history; reuse blocked. | NIST says do not force periodic changes; change only on evidence of compromise. CHECK |
| Lockout | Lock after a few failed attempts; admin unlocks manually in high-security networks. | Rate-limit failed attempts; avoid lockouts that let attackers deny access to real users. CHECK |
| Screensaver and BIOS/UEFI | Require passwords for both. | Still good practice. |
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

Exam versus real life. The book contradicts itself (minimum 10 versus 8; expire every 30 days versus 30 to 45; maximum 15 characters). If an exam question follows the book, give the book's answer; if it follows current NIST ideas, the answer is length over complexity and no forced rotation. The sources I found for NIST SP 800-63B are secondary summaries, not the standard itself. UPDATED CHECK
The book's password-history example

If passwords change every two weeks, keep at least 20 in history; that blocks reuse for about 10 months (two changes a month). Checked: 20 / 2 = 10 months. Users can defeat history by changing the password many times quickly, so also set a minimum password age. BOOK
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

The weak list the book gives (do not use): the word password, names of people or pets, dictionary words, birth dates, your username, the company name, anything written on the PC, and any of these with a number added or spelled backward. A good method: use the first letters of a sentence plus a number and symbol (the book's example is tqbf4#jotld). Do not use a published example in real life. BOOK
MEMORY TIP
Security audit habit from the book: walk the office. Sticky notes, passwords on monitors and keyboards are common. BOOK
Single sign-on, local authentication, LDAP
| Topic | Key points BOOK |
| Single sign-on (SSO) | Log in once. The domain controller issues an access token listing the resources you may use. Fewer passwords means fewer sticky notes. |
| Local authentication | Verified against the machine's own user database: SAM on Windows (c:\windows\system32\config), /etc/passwd on Linux. |
| LDAP | Directory standard based on X.500. Supports DN, RDN, CN, DC and OU attributes. Uses TCP 389; LDAP over SSL uses TCP 636. |
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE
On Linux, password hashes are normally in /etc/shadow; /etc/passwd lists accounts. Not an exam point. UPDATED CHECK
Password alternatives
The book calls passwords "the lowest form of authentication". The three alternatives are certificates, multifactor authentication and biometrics. BOOK
| Alternative | Key points BOOK |

| Certificates | A digital certificate binds an identity to a public key. X.509 fields include version, serial number, issuer, validity, subject and the subject's public key. VeriSign classes 1 to 3 are the book's historical example (individuals, organisations, servers and software). |

| Multifactor authentication (MFA) | Verifies more than one factor: something you know (password), are (fingerprint, face), have (smart card), somewhere you are (location), something you do (behaviour). Two-factor = two factors; the book calls three or more multifactor. |
| Biometrics | Physical traits (hand, retina, DNA) or behaviour (typing pattern). Costly and sometimes intrusive. Errors include false positives and false negatives. |
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

The book says users are identified "in one of three ways" but then lists five items. Learn the five. Also, two things from the same category do not make MFA: a password plus a PIN are both "something you know". Cisco's v1.1 objective wording is "multifactor authentication, certificates and biometrics". UPDATED
Quick check 13.8
Q1. According to the book, which password is stronger: 62 symbols x 10 characters or 26 symbols x 10 characters?
Answer: 62 symbols x 10 characters (about 8.4 x 10^17 against 1.4 x 10^14) - a bigger character set means more combinations.
Q2. Name three password alternatives.
Answer: Certificates, MFA and biometrics - from the book and the objective.
Q3. Which two are the same factor category: password and PIN, or password and fingerprint?
Answer: Password and PIN (both something you know) - so they are not MFA.
Q4. Which TCP port does LDAP over SSL use?
Answer: 636 - plain LDAP uses 389.
Book pages 398 to 400. Concepts only; no Cisco commands. BOOK
Public Key Infrastructure (PKI)
- A system that links users to public keys and checks identity using a certificate authority (CA), like an online notary. BOOK
- Uses asymmetric cryptography: two different keys. BOOK
- To send a private message: encrypt with the receiver's public key; the receiver decrypts with their private key. BOOK
- For a digital signature: hash the message, encrypt the hash with the sender's private key; anyone with the public key can verify who signed and that the message was not changed. BOOK
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE
Two errors in the book's PKI pages. UPDATED

1. The book says symmetric cryptography "is a lot less secure". Symmetric (one shared key) is not weaker for the same key length; it is faster, but the two sides must share the key safely. Asymmetric solves key distribution but is slower. Real systems use both.
2. Figure 13.8 labels decryption "Using User Y's Public Key". Decryption of a message encrypted with a public key uses the matching private key, which the book's own text says.
Kerberos
- Created at MIT. A full security system that establishes identity at logon with strong encryption. BOOK

- Tickets (like an amusement-park ticket): client asks the authentication server for a ticket-granting ticket (TGT), uses it to request an application ticket, then presents that to the application server (five steps in Figure 13.9). BOOK
- All systems need synchronised clocks (so NTP matters). BOOK
- A single Kerberos server is a point of failure, so use redundant servers. All secret keys live in one database, which must be protected. BOOK
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)
Kerberos normally uses port 88, and servers typically allow only a small clock difference (five minutes is common in Microsoft environments). These two details are not in the book. ADDED CHECK
Quick check 13.9
Q1. In PKI, which key decrypts a message that was encrypted with your public key?
Answer: Your private key - asymmetric pair.
Q2. In Kerberos, what do you get first?
Answer: A ticket-granting ticket (TGT) - then you request application tickets.
Q3. Why do Kerberos systems need synchronised clocks?
Answer: Tickets are time-limited and refreshed, so clocks must agree - per the book.

Book pages 400 to 407. The most exam-relevant part. There are five passwords the book lists for a router: console, auxiliary, Telnet (VTY), enable password and enable secret. Line passwords secure user mode; the enable commands secure privileged mode. BOOK
Enable passwords
Book example and warning BOOK
Todd(config)# enable secret todd
Todd(config)# enable password todd
The enable password you have chosen is the same as your
enable secret. This is not recommended. Re-enter the
enable password.
- enable secret: the newer password, stored as a hash; overrides enable password.
- enable password: older, stored in clear text unless service password-encryption is on. Not used if a secret exists. The book says skip it unless old routers are involved.
- enable use-tacacs and enable last-resort: authenticate enable through TACACS, with a fallback if no server answers. Legacy options. BOOK
Line passwords
Book commands, combined BOOK
Todd(config)# line console 0
Todd(config-line)# password console
Todd(config-line)# login
Todd(config-line)# exec-timeout 0 0
Todd(config-line)# logging synchronous
Todd(config)# line vty 0 15
Todd(config-line)# password telnet
Todd(config-line)# login
Todd(config)# line aux 0
Todd(config-line)# password aux
Todd(config-line)# login
- line console 0: the one console port. password sets the password; login makes the line ask for it. Without login there is no prompt. BOOK
- exec-timeout 0 0: the console never times out. The default is 10 minutes. BOOK
- logging synchronous: stops console messages from breaking what you type. BOOK
- line vty 0 15: sets the Telnet password for 16 virtual lines. If no VTY password is set, Telnet is refused with "Password required, but none set". BOOK
- no login on a VTY line lets Telnet in with no password. The book says never do this in production. BOOK
- line aux 0: routers only (modem port). Switches have no AUX port. BOOK
- transport input ssh: disables Telnet and allows only SSH (SSH setup is in Chapter 12). BOOK
EXAM CRITICAL

From the book: you cannot type login before a password is set on that line (on IOS 12.2 and above). You get "Login disabled on line, until `password' is set". The help (?) does not work at the (config-line)# prompt for line commands; go back to global config. BOOK
WARNING
exec-timeout 0 0 means a console session never logs out. Fine in a lab, risky in production. A typical production value is a few minutes, for example exec-timeout 5 0. ADDED
Encrypting your passwords
Book output after the command BOOK
Todd(config)# service password-encryption
Todd# show running-config
enable secret 4 ykw.3/tgsOuy9.6qmgG/EeYOYgBvfX4v.S8UNA9Rddg
enable password 7 1506040800
line con 0
login
- Only enable secret is protected by default. Other passwords appear in clear text in show running-config. BOOK
- service password-encryption: scrambles all current and future plain passwords (they show as 7). BOOK
- The book says you can turn the service off after a show run; the passwords stay encrypted. New passwords entered afterwards would be clear again. BOOK
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

Password types matter. Per Cisco's own Trust Center page, type 7 (what service password-encryption creates) is weak and reversible (Vigen�re cipher), so treat it as obfuscation, not encryption. Types 8, 9 and 10 are the secure, non-reversible choices. The book's output shows enable secret 4; type 4 is deprecated and considered weak and should not be used. UPDATED CHECK
The book says "Nicely done - the passwords will now be encrypted". Better wording: they are obscured. Prefer secret commands. UPDATED
Strong hashing (type 9) ADDED CHECK
Todd(config)# enable algorithm-type scrypt secret StrongPass99
Todd(config)# username admin algorithm-type scrypt secret Cisco@Secure
- enable algorithm-type scrypt secret ...: stores the enable secret as type 9. (sha256 gives type 8.)
- username ... algorithm-type scrypt secret ...: same for local users.
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

Hardening commands the book skips (all illustrative, CHECK ): security passwords min-length 10 (minimum length), login block-for 120 attempts 3 within 60 (slow down brute force), and login on-failure log. Use username <name> privilege 15 secret <password> plus login local on the lines for per-user logins, instead of one shared line password. ADDED
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

Telnet is shown with a password in the chapter. Use SSH (Chapter 12) in real networks: Telnet sends everything, including passwords, in clear text, which is exactly the eavesdropping problem in Section 13.2. UPDATED
Quick check 13.10
Q1. Which password wins if both enable secret and enable password are set?
Answer: enable secret - the password is ignored.
Q2. You configure password cisco on the VTY lines but forget login. What happens?
Answer: No password prompt; the line does not ask for the password - login makes it check.
Q3. What does no login on a VTY line do?
Answer: Allows Telnet with no password - the book says never use it in production.
Q4. Which type of stored password does service password-encryption create, and is it strong?
Answer: Type 7, which is reversible and weak - treat it as obscuring only.
Q5. What is the console exec-timeout default?
Answer: 10 minutes - 0 0 disables it.

labs.title: Local AAA, then RADIUS or TACACS+

content.text: - Create a local user: username admin privilege 15 secret LabPass123.
- Enable aaa new-model and aaa authentication login default local. Telnet or SSH in as admin.
- If your simulator has an AAA server, add it as radius server or tacacs server, put it in a server group, and set aaa authentication login default group <group> local.
- Stop or unplug the server and confirm you can still log in with the local user.
- Give the server a wrong key and watch the failure.
Key commands CHECK
R1(config)# username admin privilege 15 secret LabPass123
R1(config)# aaa new-model
R1(config)# aaa authentication login default local
R1(config)# radius server LAB
R1(config-radius-server)# address ipv4 10.0.0.50
R1(config-radius-server)# key labkey
R1(config)# aaa group server radius LABGRP
R1(config-sg-radius)# server name LAB
R1(config)# aaa authentication login default group LABGRP local
- The local user is created first so you cannot lock yourself out.
- aaa authentication login default group LABGRP local: server first, local as fallback.
Expected result: with the server up, logins are checked there; with it down, the local user works after a delay. CHECK
- Topology: switch SW1, a router or server acting as DHCP server on Gi0/1, two PCs on Fa0/2 and Fa0/3, and a second device on Fa0/4 to act as the rogue DHCP server.
- Configure port security on Fa0/2 with maximum 1, sticky and violation shutdown. Connect a second MAC and watch the port go err-disabled.
- Enable DHCP snooping for the VLAN; trust only Gi0/1. Start a DHCP server on the rogue device and check clients still get the real address.
- Check show ip dhcp snooping binding.
- Enable DAI on the VLAN, trust Gi0/1, and check show ip arp inspection.
Key commands CHECK
SW1(config)# ip dhcp snooping
SW1(config)# ip dhcp snooping vlan 1
SW1(config)# interface gi0/1
SW1(config-if)# ip dhcp snooping trust
SW1(config-if)# ip arp inspection trust
SW1(config)# ip arp inspection vlan 1
- Only Gi0/1 (to the real DHCP server) is trusted.
- Rogue DHCP offers from Fa0/4 are dropped because Fa0/4 is untrusted.
Expected result: the rogue server's offers never reach the clients; show ip dhcp snooping binding lists the real leases; ARP from untrusted ports without a matching binding is dropped. CHECK

content.text: Q1 Which threat type is the hardest to stop, according to the book?
A. Unstructured
B. Structured
C. External
D. Internal
Answer: D - internal users are already authorised.
Q2 A port scan to list open services is which attack category?
Answer: Reconnaissance - it discovers, it does not yet attack.
Q3 What is a vulnerability, in one line?
Answer: A - weakness that could be used to cause harm - an exploit is the way of using it.
Q1 Which Cisco IOS feature protects TCP servers from SYN floods?
A. Lock and Key
B. TCP intercept
C. CBAC
D. CHAP
Answer: B - the book's review answer 12.
Q2 Which control stops outside attackers from spoofing your internal addresses?
Answer: A - n ACL on the Internet-facing interface denying your internal range as source - the book's masquerade fix.
Q3 What is the difference between a virus and a worm?
Answer: A - virus needs human action to spread; a worm spreads by itself - both replicate.
Q4 Which attack sends echo requests to a broadcast address using the victim's address as source?
Answer: Smurf - fraggle is the UDP version.
Q5 Which term means you can prove a communication took place?
Answer: Non-repudiation - repudiation is denying it.
Q1 Name the three security program elements.
Answer: User awareness, training and physical access control - the book's list.
Q2 What is the difference between phishing and pharming?
Answer: Phishing tricks the user; pharming redirects them by corrupting DNS - pharming does not need the user to click a bad link.
Q3 Which physical control uses two interlocking doors?
A. Smart card
B. Mantrap
C. Badge reader
D. Door lock
Answer: B - a small room between two doors.
Q1 Which feature must be running for DAI to build its IP-to-MAC checks?
A. Port security
B. DHCP snooping
D. Storm control
Answer: B - the binding database comes from DHCP snooping.
Q2 Which switch ports should be DHCP-snooping trusted?
Answer: The port to the real DHCP server and uplinks toward it - never user ports.
Q3 Which port-security violation mode shuts the port down?
Answer: shutdown - it is the default mode.
Q4 Which three 802.1X roles does the book name?
Answer: C - lient (supplicant), authenticator, authentication server - RADIUS is the usual server.
Q5 A rogue DHCP server is plugged into an access port. What happens with snooping on?
Answer: Its DHCP offers are dropped on the untrusted port - only trusted ports may send offers.
Q1 A log shows which commands each admin typed. Which AAA function is that?
Answer: A - ccounting - it records what the user did.
Q2 Which comes first: authorization or authentication?
Answer: A - uthentication - you must prove identity first.
Q1 Which command enables the AAA commands on a router or switch?
A. aaa enable
B. enable aaa
C. new-model aaa
D. aaa new-model
Answer: D - the book's review answer 1.
Q2 Which protocol uses TCP and separates authentication, authorization and accounting?
Answer: TACACS+ - RADIUS uses UDP and combines authentication and authorization.
Q3 What does local at the end of aaa authentication login default group MyRadiusGroup local do?
Answer: Gives a fallback to the local user database if the RADIUS server does not respond - no answer from the server.
Q4 Which parts of a RADIUS access-request are encrypted?
Answer: Only the password - the rest is clear.
Q5 Why create a local user before aaa new-model?
Answer: So you cannot be locked out - without it you may need password recovery.
Q1 Which is the best way to handle an account when an employee leaves?
A. Leave it
B. Delete it
C. Disable it
D. Rename it to Guest
Answer: C - keeps the ID and settings without allowing logins.
Q2 Why limit simultaneous connections?
Answer: Two places at once suggests someone else is using the account - per the book.
Q1 According to the book, which password is stronger: 62 symbols x 10 characters or 26 symbols x 10 characters?
Answer: 62 symbols x 10 characters (about 8.4 x 10^17 against 1.4 x 10^14) - a bigger character set means more combinations.
Q2 Name three password alternatives.
Answer: C - ertificates, MFA and biometrics - from the book and the objective.
Q3 Which two are the same factor category: password and PIN, or password and fingerprint?
Answer: Password and PIN (both something you know) - so they are not MFA.
Q4 Which TCP port does LDAP over SSL use?
Answer: 636 - plain LDAP uses 389.
Q1 In PKI, which key decrypts a message that was encrypted with your public key?
Answer: Your private key - asymmetric pair.
Q2 In Kerberos, what do you get first?
Answer: A - ticket-granting ticket (TGT) - then you request application tickets.
Q3 Why do Kerberos systems need synchronised clocks?
Answer: Tickets are time-limited and refreshed, so clocks must agree - per the book.
Q1 Which password wins if both enable secret and enable password are set?
Answer: enable secret - the password is ignored.
Q2 You configure password cisco on the VTY lines but forget login. What happens?
Answer: No password prompt; the line does not ask for the password - login makes it check.
Q3 What does no login on a VTY line do?
Answer: A - llows Telnet with no password - the book says never use it in production.
Q4 Which type of stored password does service password-encryption create, and is it strong?
Answer: Type 7, which is reversible and weak - treat it as obscuring only.
Q5 What is the console exec-timeout default?
Answer: 10 minutes - 0 0 disables it.
Q1 Which command enables the AAA command set?
A. aaa enable
B. aaa new-model
C. enable aaa
D. aaa on
Answer: B - aaa new-model.
Q2 Which protocol uses TCP and separates authentication from authorization?
A. RADIUS
B. TACACS+
C. LDAP
D. Kerberos
Answer: B - TACACS+.
Q3 Which two statements about RADIUS are true?
A. Uses UDP
B. Uses TCP
C. Combines authentication and authorization
D. Encrypts the entire packet
Answer: A - and C - UDP; combined A and A; only the password is encrypted.
Q4 Which RADIUS reply asks the user for more information?
A. Accept
B. Reject
C. Challenge
D. Change Password
Answer: C - Challenge.
Q5 What is the correct order of AAA functions?
Answer: A - uthentication, authorization, accounting - who, what, what did.
Q6 Which command gives local fallback for RADIUS logins?
A. aaa authentication login default group G local
B. aaa authentication login local group G
C. aaa authentication fallback local
D. aaa new-model local
Answer: A - method list order matters.
Q7 Which feature builds a table of MAC, IP, VLAN, interface and lease?
A. DAI
B. Port security
C. DHCP snooping
Answer: C - the DHCP snooping binding database.
Q8 Which feature needs that table to stop ARP poisoning?
Answer: D - ynamic ARP Inspection - it checks ARP against the bindings.
Q9 Which ports should be DHCP-snooping trusted?
Answer: Uplinks and the port to the real DHCP server - not user ports.
Q10 Which port-security violation mode drops frames without logging?
A. protect
B. restrict
C. shutdown
D. sticky
Answer: A - restrict logs; shutdown err-disables.
Q11 Name the three 802.1X roles.
Answer: Supplicant (client), authenticator, authentication server - the server is usually RADIUS.
Q12 What is the name of the attack where echo requests go to a broadcast address with a spoofed source?
Answer: Smurf - fraggle uses UDP.
Q13 Which attack category is a port scan?
A. Reconnaissance
B. Access
C. DoS
D. Repudiation
Answer: A - it discovers the network.
Q14 Name the three security program elements.
Answer: User awareness, training, physical access control - per the book.
Q15 Which is a password alternative: certificates, malware lookups or screensavers?
Answer: C - ertificates - plus MFA and biometrics.
Q16 Which two factors would a password and a fingerprint be?
Answer: Something you know and something you are - two different categories, so two-factor.
Q17 In PKI, which key signs a message hash?
A. Sender's public key
B. Sender's private key
C. Receiver's public key
D. Receiver's private key
Answer: B - the signer's private key.
Q18 Which Kerberos item do you request first?
Answer: Ticket-granting ticket (TGT) - then an application ticket.
Q19 If both enable secret and enable password are configured, which is used?
Answer: enable secret -
Q20 What does login do under line vty 0 15 after password cisco?
Answer: Makes the line prompt for that password - without it, no prompt.
Q21 How does service password-encryption store passwords?
Answer: A - s type 7, which is weak and reversible - use secret or type 8 or 9.
Q22 What is the default console exec-timeout?
A. 1 minute
B. 5 minutes
C. 10 minutes
D. Never
Answer: C - 0 0 means never.
Q23 Which command allows only SSH on the VTY lines?
Answer: transport input ssh - Telnet is then refused.
Q24 Why create a local user before aaa new-model?
Answer: To avoid lockout if the server is unreachable - the console is exempt per the book.
Q25 Which TCP port does LDAP over SSL use?
Answer: B - 636 (389 is plain LDAP, 88 Kerberos, 49 TACACS+).
